analysis.one_liner: Requires asbestos bankruptcy trusts to publicly report every claimant's name and exposure history quarterly.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Judiciary Committee with no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote before the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When companies facing many asbestos lawsuits go through bankruptcy, they set up trusts to pay injured workers. This bill would require those trusts to file quarterly reports on a public court docket naming every claimant, their exposure history, and the basis for any payment, and to hand that information to any party in an asbestos lawsuit who asks for it. Supporters framed it as fraud prevention; in practice the information would flow mainly to the corporations defending asbestos lawsuits. The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.who_benefits: Corporations facing asbestos liability and their insurers would gain access to claimants' names, exposure histories, and payment records, which they could use in court and in settlement negotiations. Courts and trustees would also get better data to detect duplicate or fraudulent claims across trusts.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Asbestos defendant companies and their insurers

how_it_helps.text: Trusts must file quarterly reports on the public court docket describing each claimant's name, exposure history, and the basis for any payment, excluding confidential medical records and full Social Security numbers.

Upon written request, a trust must provide payment and demand information to any party to any lawsuit concerning asbestos liability, subject to protective orders, giving defendants in asbestos cases direct access to claim data.
Cross-checking shared payment data would let courts and bankruptcy trustees detect claims filed with multiple trusts, protecting trust assets for legitimate claimants.

analysis.who_pays: Asbestos victims and their families, whose claims, names, and exposure histories would be published quarterly and handed to the companies they are suing, and the trusts themselves, which would bear new reporting and compliance costs on every payment.

drawbacks.text: Publishing every claimant's name and exposure history on a public docket exposes seriously ill people and their families to privacy and solicitation risks, even with medical records and full Social Security numbers excluded.
Handing trust payment data to any party in an asbestos lawsuit gives defendant companies information to contest claims and pressure sick claimants into accepting smaller settlements.
Quarterly reporting on every demand and payment adds administrative burden to trusts that exist to pay victims quickly, which could delay or reduce payouts.

The strongest objection in its favor: duplicate and inflated claims against asbestos trusts are a documented problem, and disclosure could deter fraud that drains money meant for genuinely sick workers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real transparency case: trust fraud hurts legitimate claimants, and shared data can catch it. But the bill's design points the information mainly at defendant companies rather than at auditors or courts, and its practical effect would be to expose victims' identities and histories to the corporations fighting their claims while adding delay to an already slow compensation system. The burden falls on sick people; the benefit flows to their opponents in court.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Coburn introduced the bill on May 10, 2012, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee.
The Judiciary Committee held no hearing or markup, the bill never reached the Senate floor, and it expired with the end of the 112th Congress on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Asbestos victims and their families are better off that the bill died: no new quarterly public disclosures of claimants' identities and exposure histories, and no obligation to hand claim files to defendant companies. Defendant corporations gained nothing, and the existing compensation system continues unchanged.

for.name: Sen. Tom Coburn
for.role: U.S. Senator from Oklahoma; sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill; it was read twice and referred to committee.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action: no hearing, no markup, no vote; the bill died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: There was no vote to break down by party, and the bill's only sign of support was a single Republican sponsor with zero cosponsors of either party.

industries.note: The bill would hand these companies claimants' names, exposure histories, and payment data on request, information they could use to contest and settle claims for less. Their interest runs against sick workers seeking compensation.
Insurers on the hook for asbestos judgments would get the same claim data to reduce what they pay out.
Trusts that pay victims would bear new quarterly reporting and record-production duties on every demand, adding cost and delay to the system that compensates sick workers.
Lawyers who file asbestos claims would see claim data handed to opposing parties, weakening their clients' position in litigation and settlement.
